misconceptions.description: Treating ease of use for typical students as proof that the tool is accessible to all learners
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites smooth general use as evidence of accessibility
misconceptions.feedback: Usability is the typical-user experience. Accessibility asks whether learners using assistive technology or accommodations can do the same tasks. Check that separately.

misconceptions.description: Accepting a WCAG or accessibility marketing badge as proof of conformance for the classroom workflow
misconceptions.trigger: learner trusts an accessibility label without a report or task check
misconceptions.feedback: A badge is a claim. Ask for a conformance report and check the actual tasks your students perform before trusting it.

misconceptions.description: Treating an automated or AI accessibility scan as a complete accessibility clearance
misconceptions.trigger: learner reports 'no issues found' from an automated tool as final
misconceptions.feedback: Automated scans catch only some barriers. Add a task walkthrough with assistive technology and, where possible, disabled-user testing.

misconceptions.description: Assuming that a tool clearing accessibility standards therefore poses no equity risk
misconceptions.trigger: learner stops the equity analysis once accessibility is confirmed
misconceptions.feedback: An accessible tool can still impose unequal burdens, such as home connectivity or device requirements. Name those burdens and how the decision addresses them.
